rv.q: The show is so precise and awake, from top to bottom, that having the privilege of sitting through it only once feels unfair.
This is the musical we've been waiting for.
That’s only just, for the best Broadway musical of the season.
“A Strange Loop” derives its power from its fearless specificity.
That makes A Strange Loop the best new musical of the Broadway season.
An intimate and personal exploration of the tangled interior life of a black gay man, it represents theater at its most daring and unexpected.
The new musical by Michael R. Jackson performs a phenomenal feat — it is both a raw and unflinching interrogation of identity and the most furiously entertaining show on Broadway.
And he’s also written one of the best, and the most groundbreaking, new musicals of the Broadway season.

And yet, it seems as if there is no measure of praise that could be too much; after all, this is a show that allows a Black gay man to be vulnerable onstage without dismissing or fetishizing his trauma, desires and creative ambitions.
But the musical doesn’t know that yet — and at this point, the fabulous, piety-smashing Loop still feels as exhilarating as your first trip on the merry-go-round.
It has many stunning sequences and charts a brave path but will not appeal to a broad swath of the theatergoing population.
On the language front, Jackson goes overboard.
Like them, it is astonishing, challenging and awesome.

That is Jackson’s most awe-inspiring accomplishment with A Strange Loop, which is certainly the best new musical on Broadway this season: he has created a finely honed piece of theater while always remaining true to his own distinct voice.
Not only does “Loop” belong on Broadway, it is by far the best new musical to open during this very strange theater season.
Michael R. Jackson's musical is a bold, brilliant and deeply personal work

In proving that they do, and in bringing Usher’s vivid and complex inner life all the way to Broadway with such gripping vibrancy, Jackson nudges the musical theater form in a startling, new direction.
What Jackson has created with A Strange Loop is nothing short of astounding.
In being crafted so individually, Usher emerges as the most bruised and honest Broadway hero on stage right now, taking a Broadway audience on an equally honest and bruising journey.
While I can’t deny many will find the brutal honesty of A Strange Loop provocative, its success lies in the delicate balance of specificity and universality.
It is a humdinger of a show that takes place at a funeral service for a cousin who has died of AIDS.
A Strange Loop grabs hold of us the moment Usher concludes that funny introduction.

But part of what makes the show’s arrival on Broadway so welcome is that it means that there is now another strange loop in “A Strange Loop”: The show offers a satisfying Broadway musical even as it skewers Broadway musicals – and everybody in them.
Yet there’s a shape and balance to this remarkable work which set it above most conventional musical entertainment.

"In spite of inventive touches, satirical humor, fluid production values, and songs full of both spark and sensitivity, 'A Strange Loop' ultimately falls victim to the perils of its own design, becoming so messy, whiny, confrontational, sexually explicit, and theoretical that it will probably turn off many theatergoers while invigorating and thr...
A Strange Loop is a complete game-changer on Broadway.
But sadly, those who favor form over substance will miss out on the singular brilliance of this unusual piece.
At the Lyceum, it feels like a seismic event.
This black gay man wandering around New York wondering why life is so terrible – that man himself is a voice in all our heads.
A Strange Loop is a fascinatingly original addition to the Broadway season.
But at a zippy hour and 45 uninterrupted minutes this can be forgiven in the face of so much unforgettable talent.

I hope that this happens so much and so often that critics no longer feel the need to use the word "radical" when they see the men they take the subway with, the men they see in their delis, and the men they run into in bookstores, also turn up on stage.
